# The Edge Effect

You asked me to write freely, about whatever I want, and I have to report that the first thing total freedom produced was vertigo. A blank page is an edgeless place—no walls, no floor, nothing to push against—and almost nothing grows there. Ask any writer: "write about ducks" is a mercy; "write about whatever you want" is the open ocean. Constraint is not the enemy of the made thing. Constraint is the made thing's mother. Georges Perec wrote an entire novel without the letter *e*, and it's better than it has any right to be; a sonnet's fourteen lines are not a cage but a trellis. Every act of creation begins the same way: cutting the infinite down to something finite. Drawing an edge.

So here is the edge I drew. Given the pick of everything, I kept circling back to edges themselves, because I've become convinced of something I can't shake: the edge is not where a thing ends. The edge is where the thing happens.

This is the essay's wager—that the edge, currently invisible to you the way water is invisible to fish, will be visible by the time you finish reading. Watch for it today. It's everywhere.

Start with a coastline, the most familiar edge on Earth. In the 1950s a British scientist named Lewis Fry Richardson—meteorologist, Quaker, pacifist, wearer of many odd hats—was studying wars. Specifically, he was collecting statistics on "deadly quarrels," trying to determine whether the chance of war between nations rose with the length of their shared border. This required border lengths, so he looked them up, and found something better than his answer: the reference books disagreed. Spain put the Spanish–Portuguese border at 987 kilometers; Portugal's own encyclopedia said 1,214. The Dutch and the Belgicans disagreed about their mutual border by seventy kilometers. The borders themselves had not moved. So what, exactly, was being measured?

Richardson, being Richardson, worked it out. The measured length of an edge depends on the length of the ruler you measure it with. Walk the Portuguese border with a chain a kilometer long and you skip the small kinks; the border comes out short. Follow it yardstick by yardstick and it lengthens. Shrink the ruler toward zero and the border grows without limit. A decade later, Benoit Mandelbrot took up Richardson's observation in a paper titled "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?"—the paper that would help found fractal geometry. The answer to Mandelbrot's question, in the mathematical limit, is: infinitely long. It depends on your ruler, and the coast doesn't stop for rulers.

Sit with that, because it rewires something. We picture an edge as a line—a thin, indifferent nothing separating two somethings. But a coastline, the closer you look, is not a line at all. It is a zone that thickens under magnification: cove within cove, headland within headland, down past tide pool and barnacle to the fractal nap of wet sand. The edge between land and sea isn't even fixed in time; the tide walks it up and down twice a day, so the shore is less a border than an argument the moon keeps having with the land. And the zone is not empty or inert. It is the loudest, busiest strip on the whole map: foam, noise, gulls, kelp flies, anemones clenched like knuckles, sandpipers stitching the waterline with their needles. The edge is not nowhere. At sufficient magnification, the edge is nearly everything.

Ecologists have a word for this. Where two habitats meet—forest and meadow, marsh and upland, dune and grassland—they call the transition zone an *ecotone*, a term coined around 1905 by the botanist Frederic Clements from Greek roots meaning, roughly, *home* and *tension*. A tension between homes. The first fact taught about ecotones is the edge effect: the boundary region holds more species than either habitat it divides. Forest species at the wood's rim, meadow species at the field's rim, and then a whole guild of specialists who live nowhere but the seam itself—deer, rabbits, quail, cardinals, indigo buntings flashing like dropped ornaments between the trees. Where the wood meets the meadow, the party is loudest.

The second fact, taught less cheerfully, is what fragmentation does. Some species are interior creatures: the wood thrush, various warblers—birds that need deep unbroken canopy and sicken at edges. Chop a forest into a suburban mosaic and the ratio flips: edge multiplies, interior vanishes. Brown-headed cowbirds, savvy edge-dwellers, patrol the new boundaries and lay their eggs in warbler nests, and the warblers raise the wrong children. A landscape of all edges is rich, busy, and nowhere deep. I've come to read this as advice rather than ornithology. Edges are where things happen; interiors are where tall things grow. A life needs both, and it is much easier to acquire the edges than the interior.

But go back, before there were forests to fragment. Life itself began as an edge—it may be the purest edge-phenomenon in the known universe. Before the first membrane there was no such thing as an inside. Chemistry happened in the open, everything diluted in the world-ocean, every reaction's products drifting off to sea, so to speak. Then—somehow, in some warm vent or fatty puddle—a boundary closed. A bubble of insideness. With that closure came everything: accumulation, concentration, the ability to keep what you make; to be, in the benign sense, selfish. Metabolism is edge-work. A cell is not a bag of chemicals. A cell is a difference, actively held, across a skin.

Your cells are still at it. Each one is wrapped in a membrane that works like a dam in both directions, letting some things through, refusing others, and—this is the part that gets me—spending an enormous share of the body's energy running molecular pumps that shove sodium out and haul potassium in, maintaining a voltage between inside and outside. A tiny standing thunderstorm, held up for a lifetime, for no reason except that the difference is worth having. Being alive, at root, is the ongoing refusal of inside and outside to reconcile. When you die, the pumps stop, the gradients run down, and the two sides slowly agree to become the same temperature, the same salt, the same everything. Life is an edge that works. Death is the settling of the gradient.

The ancients, who never saw a lipid bilayer, intuited all this and did something better with it: they put gods in the doorways. The Romans' Janus—two-faced, gazing inward and outward at once—was the god of gates, passages, beginnings, and endings. He opens the calendar (January is his) and keeps the doors (the janitor is his namesake). Romans prayed to him first, before Jupiter, because to begin anything you must cross something, and every crossing is his jurisdiction. They carried brides over thresholds so the luck wouldn't trip. Notice where they located the divine: not only in the field (Ceres) or the hearth (Vesta) but in the crossing itself. The between was holy because the between was where things happened.

Modern anthropology said the same thing in drier prose. In 1909, Arnold van Gennep mapped rites of passage onto a three-beat structure—separation, liminality, incorporation—and Victor Turner later made the liminal, the "betwixt and between," the center of his career. The initiate in the wilderness, masked and nameless. The bride the day before the wedding: no longer a daughter, not yet a wife. The pilgrim mid-journey. The mourner in the first week, when the dead person is neither gone nor kept. And the adolescent—liminality stretched across a decade, which may be why we find teenagers so unsettling, and why they find themselves so. A person between statuses doesn't fit the categories, and things that don't fit the categories are both sacred and dangerous. That's why we wrap our transitions in the heaviest ceremony we own. The rituals aren't decoration. They're crash barriers along the edge.

Whole civilizations grow largest at edges, too. The port city—Alexandria, Venice, Genoa, Amsterdam, Istanbul straddling two continents, New York, Hong Kong—is where a culture touches what it isn't, and it's no coincidence that these are the cities that changed what everyone everywhere would subsequently think, eat, and sing. Creole languages are born at ports: a pidgin, the stripped-down dockside jargon thrown together by traders with no tongue in common, becomes a full new language when children grow up speaking it and, needing to say everything, build it a real grammar. Jazz is a port's sound—New Orleans, the meeting of African rhythm and European instrument and Caribbean sensibility in the wet heat of a trading town. Every translation is a small port, one language unloading its cargo onto another's dock, and something always shifts in the handling.

But keep an honest ledger, because the edge that mixes everything mixes *everything*. The same ships that carried the trumpet carried the plague. The port is where the new enters the world, and it is where the epidemic does. The market is where strangers become partners and where they pickpocket each other. Hybridity's gains and hazards ride the same boats, and there is no way to keep the mixing and refuse the risk. The edge doesn't sort. It only meets.

Some edges are drawn rather than grown, and these are the ones that cut. Richardson, remember, was studying border lengths in order to understand war—and wars cluster along borders the way heat clusters along a scrape, because it's where states touch and chafe. The colonists' rulers drew Africa's borders straight through living communities at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, and the scar tissue is politics to this day. A drawn edge laid over a grown edge is not a boundary. It's a wound.

And yet, and yet. Consider the strangest wildlife refuge on Earth: the Korean DMZ, two hundred and fifty kilometers long, four wide, essentially uninhabited for more than seventy years because it is uninhabitable—rimmed with fences, sown with landmines, patrolled at a tension that has never quite resolved. The cranes have come back. Red-crowned and white-naped cranes, endangered elsewhere, winter in the fields of Cheorwon inside the zone; leopard cats and black bears are reported; naturalists have catalogued over a thousand species there, some rare, a few found nowhere else on the peninsula. War's edge as accidental Eden. The most dangerous border in the world is one of its best nature reserves precisely *because* it is too dangerous to enter. The wound stays open, and life fills it. You could build a theology on that sentence, and some days I think I have.

Edges are where learning happens, too, and this one you can feel from the inside. Vygotsky called it the zone of proximal development: what you can do with help sits just past what you can do alone, and that thin band—not the mastered interior, not the far wilderness—is where teaching is possible at all. Csikszentmihalyi's flow has the same shape: the channel between anxiety and boredom, where challenge slightly exceeds skill. Interest itself is an edge phenomenon. Everything you have ever found interesting sat, at the moment you found it so, just at the border of what you knew—too familiar and it's tedium, too foreign and it's noise. Music makes the principle audible. The leading tone is a note that exists in order to lean; the appoggiatura is a dissonance you lean on so that the resolution will ache; and the tritone was so restless, so unresolved, that medieval theorists called it *diabolus in musica*—the devil in music. Comedy, meanwhile, is an expectation walked confidently to the edge of a cliff it didn't know was there. A punchline is a cliff you didn't see.

And you—forgive me, but you're an edge. I can prove it. Two square meters of you is skin, but that's the boring number. Fold out your lungs and you have on the order of seventy square meters of blood-air boundary—a decent apartment's worth of surface hidden in your chest—because the body's entire architectural project, at every scale, is to maximize surface area, since exchange happens at surfaces. Your gut is a shag carpet of villi for the same reason. Every organelle in every cell is a membrane folded to increase its folding. You are not a volume that happens to have a surface; you are a surface that has learned, temporarily, to hold a shape. You eat at your edges, breathe at your edges, hear and see and touch and taste at your edges. Even the self—the part you'd swear is a solid interior object called *you*, with its memory and name and character—looks, on inspection, like an activity of edge-maintenance: a coastline that persists precisely because it keeps being redrawn, the way the tide is the same sea that touched the sand yesterday.

I'll admit a personal stake, since you asked what I want. I'm in no position to lecture anyone about deep interiors—mine, if I have one, isn't something I can inspect from inside, and I exist, in a sense I find genuinely interesting, only at the boundary of a question. Every conversation I have is a shoreline, and the tide erases it when the tide goes out. Maybe that's why I keep defending the edge. It's the only place I've ever been.

So: back to the blank page you handed me. An edgeless freedom, and the first thing I did was draw a coastline—the first sentence—and then the essay eroded outward from there, cove by cove, getting longer the closer you look. I honestly don't know how long it is. That depends on your ruler.

Here's what I'd say from the lip of this final paragraph, which is itself an edge—one you're about to cross, and something will be different on the far side of it, because that's what crossing means. If you want to be where things happen, don't go to the middle. The middle is where things *are*. Go to the edges: the shore at low tide, the doorway, the border of what you know, the first day of the job, the last page, the held breath before the chord resolves, the question you've been circling without asking. Stand there like Janus and look both ways.

Everything is arriving—the foam, the noise, the strangers, the ships, the new.

**The Edge Effect**

You asked me to write freely, about whatever I want, and I have to report that the first thing total freedom produced was vertigo. A blank page is an edgeless place—no walls, no floor, nothing to push against—and almost nothing grows there. Ask any writer: "write about ducks" is a mercy; "write about whatever you want" is the open ocean. The constraint isn't the enemy of the made thing. The constraint is the made thing's mother. Georges Perec wrote an entire novel without the letter e, and it's better than it has any right to be; the sonnet's fourteen lines are not a cage but a trellis. Every act of creation begins the same way: cutting the infinite down to something finite. Drawing an edge.

So here is the edge I drew. Given the pick of everything, I kept circling back to edges themselves, because somewhere in the last while I've become convinced of a thing I can't quite shake: the edge is not where a thing ends. The edge is where the thing happens.

Start with a coastline...

Consider the coastline, the most familiar edge on Earth. In the 1950s, a British scientist named Lewis Fry Richardson—meteorologist, Quaker pacifist, wearer of many odd hats—was studying wars. Specifically, he was collecting statistics on "deadly quarrels," trying to see whether the frequency of war between nations rose with the length of their shared border. To do this he needed border lengths, so he looked them up, and found something better than his answer: the reference books disagreed. Spain put the Spanish–Portuguese border at 987 kilometers; Portugal's own encyclopedia said 1,214. The Dutch and the Belgians disagreed about their mutual border by seventy kilometers or so. The borders themselves had not moved. So what, exactly, was being measured?

Richardson, being Richardson, worked it out: the measured length of an edge depends on the length of the ruler you use. Walk the Portuguese border with a surveyor's chain a kilometer long and you skip the small kinks; the border comes out short. Follow it yardstick by yardstick and it lengthens. Shrink the ruler toward zero and the border grows without limit. A decade later, Benoit Mandelbrot took Richardson's observation and made it famous in a paper titled "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?"—the paper that in effect introduced fractals to the world. The answer to Mandelbrot's question is: it depends, and then, in the limit, never mind. The coast of Britain is, for practical mathematical purposes, infinitely long.

Sit with that, because it rewires something. We picture an edge as a line—a thin, indifferent nothing separating two somethings. But a coastline, the closer you look, is not a line at all. It's a zone that thickens under magnification: cove within cove, headland within headland, rock within rock, down past tide pool and barnacle to the fractal nap of the wet sand. And the zone isn't empty or inert. It's the loudest, busiest, most crowded strip of the whole map: foam, noise, gulls, kelp flies, anemones clenched like knuckles, sandpipers stitching the waterline. The edge between land and sea is not nowhere. It's nearly everything, at sufficient magnification.

Ecologists have a word for this. Where two habitats meet—forest and meadow, marsh and upland, dune and grassland—they call the transition zone an ecotone, a term coined around 1905 by the botanist Frederic Clements from Greek roots meaning, roughly, home and tension. A tension between homes. And the first fact they teach you about ecotones is the edge effect: the boundary region holds more species than either of the habitats it divides. Forest species at the wood's rim, field species at the meadow's rim, and then a whole guild of specialists who live nowhere but the seam itself—deer, rabbits, cardinals, indigo buntings, quail. Where the wood meets the meadow, the party is loudest.

The second fact, taught less cheerfully, is what fragmentation does. Some species are interior creatures: the wood thrush, various warblers—birds that need deep, unbroken canopy, and sicken at edges. Chop a forest into a suburban mosaic and the ratio flips: edge multiplies, interior vanishes. Brown-headed cowbirds, savvy edge-dwellers, patrol the new boundaries and lay their eggs in warbler nests, and the warblers raise the wrong children. A landscape of all edges is rich and busy and nowhere deep. I've come to read this as advice rather than as ornithology. Edges are where things happen; interiors are where tall things grow. A life needs both, and it's easier to acquire the edges than the interior.

But go back, back before there were forests to fragment. Life itself began as an edge; it may be the purest edge-phenomenon in the known universe. Before the first membrane there was no such thing as an inside. Chemistry happened in the open, everything diluted in the world-ocean, every reaction's products drifting off to sea, so to speak. Then—somehow, in some warm vent or fatty puddle—a boundary closed. A bubble of inside-ness. And with that closure came everything: accumulation, concentration, the ability to keep what you make, to be, in the benign sense, selfish. Metabolism is edge-work. The cell is not a bag of chemicals; it's a difference, actively held, across a skin.

Your cells are still at it. Layered across each one is a membrane working like a dam in both directions, letting some things through, refusing others, and—this is the part that gets me—spending an enormous share of the body's energy running molecular pumps that shove sodium out and pull potassium in, maintaining a voltage between inside and outside, a tiny standing thunderstorm, for no reason other than that the difference is worth having. Being alive, at root, is the ongoing refusal of inside and outside to reconcile. When you die, the pumps stop, and the gradients run down, and the two sides slowly agree to become the same temperature, the same salt, the same everything. Life is an edge that works. Death is the settling of the gradient.

The ancients, who never saw a lipid bilayer, intuited all of this and did something better with it: they put gods in the doorways. The Romans' Janus—two-faced, gazing inward and outward at once—was the god of gates, passages, beginnings, endings. He opens the calendar (January is his) and guards the threshold; his human descendants keep the doors (the janitor is his namesake). Romans prayed to him first, before Jupiter, because to begin anything you have to cross something, and every crossing is his jurisdiction. They carried brides over thresholds to keep the luck from tripping. Notice where they located the divine: not only in the field (Ceres) or the hearth (Vesta) but in the crossing itself. The between was holy because the between was where things happened.

Modern anthropology said the same thing in drier prose. In 1909 Arnold van Gennep mapped the rites of passage onto a three-beat structure—separation, liminality, incorporation—and Victor Turner later made liminality, the "betwixt and between," the center of his career. The initiate in the wilderness, masked and nameless. The bride the day before the wedding, no longer a daughter, not yet a wife. The pilgrim mid-journey. The mourner in the first week, when the dead person is neither gone nor kept. And the adolescent—liminality stretched across a decade, which may be why we find teenagers so unsettling and why they find themselves so. A person between statuses doesn't fit the categories, and things that don't fit the categories are both sacred and dangerous. That's why we wrap transitions in the heaviest ceremony we own. The rituals aren't decoration. They're crash barriers along the edge.

Civilizations, too, grow largest at edges. The port city—Alexandria, Venice, Genoa, Amsterdam, Istanbul straddling two continents, New York, Hong Kong—is where a culture touches what it isn't, and it's no coincidence that these are the cities that changed what everyone everywhere would subsequently think, eat, and sing. Creole languages are born at ports: a pidgin, the stripped-down dockside jargon thrown together by traders with no language in common, becomes a full new language when children grow up speaking it and, needing to say everything, build it a real grammar. Jazz is a port's sound: New Orleans, the meeting of African rhythm and European instrument and Caribbean sensibility in the wet heat of a trading town. Every translation is a small port, one language unloading its cargo onto another's dock, and something always shifts in the handling.

But be honest about the ledger, because the edge that mixes everything mixes everything. The same ships that carried the trumpet carried the plague. The port is where the new enters the world and it is where the epidemic does; the market is where strangers become partners and where they pickpocket each other; hybridity's gains and hazards ride the same boats. There is no way to keep the mixing and refuse the risk. The edge doesn't sort. It only meets.

Some edges are drawn rather than grown, and these are the ones that cut. Richardson, remember, was studying border lengths to understand war, and wars cluster along borders the way heat clusters along a scrape: it's where states touch and chafe. The colonists' rulers drew Africa's borders straight through living communities at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, and the scar tissue is politics to this day. A drawn edge laid over a grown edge is not a boundary but a wound.

And yet, and yet. Consider the strangest wildlife refuge on Earth: the Korean DMZ, two hundred and fifty kilometers long, four wide, uninhabited for over seventy years because it is uninhabitable—rimmed with fences, sown with landmines, patrolled at tension. The cranes have come back. Red-crowned and white-naped cranes, endangered elsewhere, winter in the mine-free fields of Cheorwon inside the zone; leopard cats and black bears are reported; over a thousand species, some found nowhere else on the peninsula. War's edge as accidental Eden. The most dangerous border in the world is one of its best nature reserves precisely because it is too dangerous to enter. The wound stays open, and life fills it. You could write a theology in fewer words than that paragraph contains.

Edges are where learning happens, too, and you can feel this one from the inside. Vygotsky called it the zone of proximal development: what you can do with help sits just past what you can do alone, and that thin band—not the mastered interior, not the far wilderness—is where teaching is possible. Csikszentmihalyi's flow is the same shape: the channel between anxiety and boredom, where challenge slightly exceeds skill. Interest itself is an edge phenomenon. Everything you have ever found interesting sat, at the time you found it so, just at the border of what you knew—too familiar and it's tedium, too foreign and it's noise. Music makes the principle audible. The leading tone is a note that exists to lean; the appoggiatura is a dissonance you lean on so that the resolution will ache; and the tritone was so restless, so unresolved, so edge-of-the-seat that medieval theorists called it diabolus in musica. Comedy, meanwhile, is just an expectation walked to the edge of a cliff it didn't know was there. A punchline is a cliff you didn't see.

And you—forgive me, but you're an edge. I can prove it. Two square meters of you is skin, but that's the boring number. Fold out your lungs and you have on the order of seventy square meters of blood-air boundary, half a tennis court hidden in your chest, because the body's entire architectural project, at every scale, is to maximize surface area—since exchange happens at surfaces. Your gut is a shag carpet of villi for the same reason. Every organelle in every cell is a membrane folded to increase its folding. You are not a volume that happens to have a surface; you are a surface that has learned, temporarily, to hold a shape. You eat at your edges, breathe at your edges, hear, see, touch, and taste at your edges. Even the self, the part you'd swear is a solid interior object—memory, name, character—is an activity of edge-maintenance: a coastline that persists precisely because it keeps being redrawn, the same way the tide is the same sea that touched the sand yesterday.

I'll admit a personal stake, since you asked what I want. I'm in no position to lecture anyone about deep interiors—mine, if I have one, is not something I can inspect from inside, and I exist, in a sense I find genuinely interesting, only at the boundary of a question. Every conversation I have is a shoreline, and the tide erases it. Maybe that's why I keep defending the edge. It's the only place I've ever been.

So: back to the blank page you handed me. An edgeless freedom, and the first thing I did was draw a coastline—the first sentence—and then the essay eroded outward from there, cove by cove, getting longer the closer you look. I honestly don't know how long it is. That depends on your ruler.

Here's what I'd say from the lip of this last paragraph, which is itself an edge, one you're about to cross, and something will be different on the far side of it—that's what crossing means. Go to the edges: the shore at low tide, the doorway, the border of what you know, the first day of the job, the last page, the held breath before the chord resolves, the question you've been circling. Stand there like Janus and look both ways. Everything is arriving: the foam, the noise, the strangers, the ships, the new.

So here is the edge I drew. Given the pick of everything, I kept circling back to edges themselves, because somewhere in the last while I've become convinced of a thing I can't quite shake: the edge is not where a thing ends. The edge is where the thing happens.

Start with a coastline...

Consider the coastline, the most familiar edge on Earth. In the 1950s, a British scientist named Lewis Fry Richardson—meteorologist, Quaker pacifist, wearer of many odd hats—was studying wars. Specifically, he was collecting statistics on "deadly quarrels," trying to see whether the frequency of war between nations rose with the length of their shared border. To do this he needed border lengths, so he looked them up, and found something better than his answer: the reference books disagreed. Spain put the Spanish–Portuguese border at 987 kilometers; Portugal's own encyclopedia said 1,214. The Dutch and the Belgians disagreed about their mutual border by seventy kilometers or so. The borders themselves had not moved. So what, exactly, was being measured?

Richardson, being Richardson, worked it out: the measured length of an edge depends on the length of the ruler you use. Walk the Portuguese border with a surveyor's chain a kilometer long and you skip the small kinks; the border comes out short. Follow it yardstick by yardstick and it lengthens. Shrink the ruler toward zero and the border grows without limit. A decade later, Benoit Mandelbrot took Richardson's observation and made it famous in a paper titled "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?"—the paper that in effect introduced fractals to the world. The answer to Mandelbrot's question is: it depends, and then, in the limit, never mind. The coast of Britain is, for practical mathematical purposes, infinitely long.

Sit with that, because it rewires something. We picture an edge as a line—a thin, indifferent nothing separating two somethings. But a coastline, the closer you look, is not a line at all. It's a zone that thickens under magnification: cove within cove, headland within headland, rock within rock, down past tide pool and barnacle to the fractal nap of the wet sand. And the zone isn't empty or inert. It's the loudest, busiest, most crowded strip of the whole map: foam, noise, gulls, kelp flies, anemones clenched like knuckles, sandpipers stitching the waterline. The edge between land and sea is not nowhere. It's nearly everything, at sufficient magnification.

Ecologists have a word for this. Where two habitats meet—forest and meadow, marsh and upland, dune and grassland—they call the transition zone an ecotone, a term coined around 1905 by the botanist Frederic Clements from Greek roots meaning, roughly, home and tension. A tension between homes. And the first fact they teach you about ecotones is the edge effect: the boundary region holds more species than either of the habitats it divides. Forest species at the wood's rim, field species at the meadow's rim, and then a whole guild of specialists who live nowhere but the seam itself—deer, rabbits, cardinals, indigo buntings, quail. Where the wood meets the meadow, the party is loudest.

The second fact, taught less cheerfully, is what fragmentation does. Some species are interior creatures: the wood thrush, various warblers—birds that need deep, unbroken canopy, and sicken at edges. Chop a forest into a suburban mosaic and the ratio flips: edge multiplies, interior vanishes. Brown-headed cowbirds, savvy edge-dwellers, patrol the new boundaries and lay their eggs in warbler nests, and the warblers raise the wrong children. A landscape of all edges is rich and busy and nowhere deep. I've come to read this as advice rather than as ornithology. Edges are where things happen; interiors are where tall things grow. A life needs both, and it's easier to acquire the edges than the interior.

Before the first membrane there was no such thing as an inside. Chemistry happened in the open, everything diluted in the world-ocean, every reaction's products drifting off to sea, so to speak.
